name: Public Provident Fund (PPF)
pros: Backed by Government of India — zero default risk
Interest earned is fully tax-free under Section 80C
Flexible partial withdrawal allowed from Year 7 onward
cons: 15-year lock-in period significantly limits liquidity
Returns are set by government and may not outpace inflation
Annual contribution capped at ₹1.5 lakh per account

name: Nifty 50 Index Fund (Direct Growth)
pros: Broad diversification across 50 large-cap Indian companies
Low expense ratio compared to actively managed funds
No lock-in — fully redeemable any business day
cons: Returns fluctuate with market conditions — can be negative in downturns
Short-term capital gains taxed at 15% if redeemed within one year
Not suitable if funds may be needed within 1–2 years

name: Bank Fixed Deposit (1-Year)
pros: Guaranteed returns with DICGC deposit insurance up to ₹5 lakh
Simple to open online — no demat account required
Interest paid quarterly, providing predictable income
cons: 1-year lock-in; premature withdrawal attracts a 1% penalty
Interest income is fully taxable at your income-tax slab rate
Returns typically do not outpace long-run inflation

name: Liquid Mutual Fund
pros: Highly liquid — redemption typically credited within one business day
Lower interest-rate risk than longer-duration debt funds
Good emergency-buffer parking option for scholarship awards
cons: Returns are lower than equity or even most FDs in the long run
Gains taxed as short-term capital gains if held under 3 years
Fund NAV can dip slightly during extreme credit events

name: Small-Cap Growth Fund (Direct)
pros: Highest historical long-run return potential among listed options
Exposure to emerging companies in fast-growing sectors
SIP option allows disciplined, rupee-cost-averaged investing
cons: High volatility — portfolio value can drop 30–50% in bear markets
Recommended minimum horizon of 5–7 years to ride out downturns
Not appropriate if the funds may be needed within the next 3 years

name: Sectoral / Thematic ETF (Technology)
pros: Targeted exposure to high-growth technology sector companies
No lock-in — traded on exchange like a stock during market hours
Lower expense ratio than actively managed sectoral funds
cons: Sector concentration risk — a single-sector downturn hits hard
Short-term capital gains taxed at 15% if sold within one year
Requires a demat account and understanding of ETF trading mechanics

name: Corporate Bond Fund (Short Duration)
pros: Higher returns than savings accounts or liquid funds with manageable risk
No lock-in period — can be redeemed in 1–3 business days
Portfolio of investment-grade corporate bonds spreads credit risk
cons: Credit risk if underlying issuers default or are downgraded
Returns fluctuate with interest rate changes
Not covered by DICGC insurance like bank deposits

name: S&P 500 Index Fund (Vanguard / Fidelity)
pros: Tracks the 500 largest US companies — broad market exposure
Ultra-low expense ratio (as low as 0.03% with major brokers)
No lock-in — can be sold on any trading day
cons: Subject to market volatility — returns can be negative in recession years
Short-term capital gains apply if sold within 12 months
Not suitable if the funds are needed within the next 1–2 years

name: Treasury I-Bond
pros: Backed by the US federal government — zero default risk
Inflation-adjusted returns protect purchasing power over time
Interest is exempt from state and local income taxes
cons: Must hold for at least 12 months; early redemption forfeits 3 months of interest
Annual purchase limit of $10,000 per Social Security number
Can only be purchased through TreasuryDirect — not tradable on open market

name: High-Yield Savings Account (HYSA)
pros: FDIC-insured up to $250,000 — effectively risk-free
Fully liquid — withdraw at any time with no penalties
Easy to open online with no minimum balance at most banks
cons: Interest rates fluctuate with the Federal Reserve benchmark rate
Returns typically lag inflation over long periods
Not intended as a long-term investment vehicle

name: Small-Cap Growth ETF (Russell 2000)
pros: Exposure to ~2,000 smaller US companies with high growth potential
No lock-in — fully tradable on any exchange trading day
Diversification across small-cap reduces single-stock risk
cons: Significantly higher volatility than large-cap indices
Can experience drawdowns of 40–60% during bear markets
Best held for 7+ years to average out short-term volatility

name: Corporate Bond ETF (Investment Grade)
pros: Higher yield than Treasury bonds with managed credit risk
Traded like a stock — liquid and accessible on any trading day
Diversifies a portfolio that already holds equity index funds
cons: Bond prices fall when interest rates rise
Corporate bonds carry default risk not present in US Treasuries
Dividend income subject to ordinary income tax rates

name: FTSE 100 Index Fund (Vanguard / iShares)
pros: Tracks the 100 largest companies listed on the London Stock Exchange
Low ongoing charge figure (OCF) — typically 0.07–0.20% per year
Internationally diversified revenue base reduces UK-specific risk
cons: Returns are subject to market fluctuations and currency risk
FTSE 100 is heavily weighted toward financials and energy sectors
Not appropriate if funds are needed within the next 2–3 years

name: Cash ISA (Fixed Rate)
pros: All interest earned is completely free of UK income tax
FSCS-protected up to £85,000 per institution
Simple to open — available via most high-street and online banks
cons: Fixed-rate terms mean early withdrawal typically incurs a loss penalty
Annual ISA allowance capped at £20,000 per tax year
Returns may trail inflation depending on the interest rate environment

name: Premium Bonds (National Savings)
pros: 100% backed by HM Treasury — no risk of losing principal
Monthly prize draws offer the chance of tax-free prizes up to £1 million
Fully accessible — encashment requests processed within 3 business days
cons: Returns are probabilistic — some holders earn well below the prize fund rate
Maximum holding capped at £50,000 per person
Not inflation-linked — purchasing power erodes if prizes fall short of inflation

name: Stocks & Shares ISA (Global Equity)
pros: All capital gains and dividends are completely tax-free within the ISA wrapper
Access to global equity markets via low-cost tracker funds
Annual allowance of £20,000 enables meaningful tax-sheltered growth
cons: Market value can fall significantly in the short term
Returns are not guaranteed and depend on global market performance
Best treated as a long-term investment with a 5–10 year horizon

name: UK Corporate Bond Fund (Short Duration)
pros: Higher yield than gilts or Cash ISAs with diversified credit exposure
Short duration reduces interest rate sensitivity compared to long-bond funds
Can be held inside an ISA wrapper for tax-efficient income
cons: Corporate bond prices fall when UK interest rates rise
Credit risk if underlying issuers are downgraded or default
Not covered by FSCS insurance in the same way as bank deposits
